title: Signatures of slow particle transport in the interacting Aubry-André chain
authors: S. Sharifan, M. Kiefer-Emmanouilidis, J. Sirker
abstract: Slow delocalization in strongly disordered many-body quantum chains can originate from two distinct mechanisms: rare resonances and avalanches, rooted in the energy statistics, or an energy-independent combinatorial path-entropy obstruction in operator space. Quasiperiodic potentials eliminate rare regions with similar potentials that are thought to be responsible for avalanche instabilities and modify the statistics of resonances, thus allowing us to delineate the two mechanisms. To do so, we numerically study the entanglement entropy $S(t)$, number entropy $S_N(t)$, and Hartley number entropy $S_H(t)$ following a quantum quench in the interacting Aubry-André chain with disorder strength $D$. We find $S(t)\simμ\ln t$, $S_N(t)\simν\ln\ln t$ with growth rates $μ\simν\sim D^{-γ}$ and $γ\approx 3$, the same behavior that was previously found in the case of quenched disorder. Furthermore, the saturation values $S_H(t\to\infty)$ continue to grow with system size $L$ as $\ln L$, a growth that persists for $D\gtrsim 8$ where MBL was argued to be stable. The similarity of the quasi-periodic and quenched disorder cases points to a common origin of the slow particle transport that does not rely on rare-region avalanches and persists despite strongly modified resonance statistics.
summary: This study investigates the origin of slow particle transport in interacting quantum chains by comparing quasi-periodic and disordered systems. Using entropy measures, the authors show that the slow dynamics observed are robust and stem from a mechanism independent of rare-region resonances. This challenges current understanding of MBL stability by identifying a universal obstruction in the thermodynamic limit.
main_problem: The paper aims to distinguish between two mechanisms causing slow particle transport in strongly disordered quantum chains: rare resonances/avalanches or an energy-independent combinatorial path-entropy obstruction.
main_result: The slow transport signatures observed in the quasi-periodic Aubry-André chain are quantitatively similar to those in quenched disorder, suggesting a common origin independent of rare-region avalanches.
method: Numerical simulation of time evolution following a quantum quench, calculating entanglement entropy, number entropy, and Hartley number entropy.
model_or_system: The interacting Aubry-André chain is studied, featuring a quasiperiodic potential $D_j = D \cos(2\pi eta j + \phi)$ applied to spinless fermions at half filling.
key_observables:
Entanglement entropy $S(t)$, Number entropy $S_N(t)$, and Hartley number entropy $S_H(t)$; their growth rates ($\mu, 
u$) and saturation values ($\ln L$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength $D$, system size $L$, and the quasiperiodicity parameter $ eta$ (golden ratio).
main_assumptions: The quasi-periodic potential is constructed to eliminate rare regions responsible for avalanche instabilities, allowing a clean test of the underlying transport mechanism.
figures_summary:
Figures illustrate the logarithmic and double-logarithmic growth of entropies ($S(t) \sim \mu \ln t$, $S_N(t) \sim 
u \ln \ln t$) and the linear growth of $S_H$ with system size ($\ln L$), comparing quasi-periodic and disordered cases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem by contrasting two theoretical origins for slow transport. It then applies numerical methods to the interacting Aubry-André chain, calculating various entropy measures. The core of the work is comparing the scaling laws and saturation behaviors between the quasi-periodic and quenched disorder limits to draw a conclusion about the universal nature of the slow transport mechanism.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the stability of Many-Body Localized (MBL) phases by providing evidence that slow transport persists even when the mechanisms previously thought necessary (like rare resonances) are explicitly removed.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
